medical.title: Lab-grown tissue reveals how inflammation may drive heart relaxation failure
medical.summary: Scientists study the underlying causes of a disease or test potential new drugs in animal models or cells obtained from human biopsy specimens before clinical trials. However, disease models in animals do not mimic actual human disease, and biopsy specimens are difficult to access for research purposes. Lab-grown tissues engineered from stem cells reprogrammed from human cells, called human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), are rapidly emerging as a more reliable and accessible model in medical research.

medical.title: Micro-LED mask improves skin elasticity beyond injections alone
medical.summary: Home beauty devices that allow users to care for their skin conveniently at home have grown popular recently, but conventional LED masks are limited by their rigid structures and point-emitting LEDs, which must be positioned away from the skin to spread light over a broader area. This inherently prevents close skin contact and increases optical loss.

medical.title: Powerful new tool reveals potential 'goldmine' of cancer targets hidden in 'junk DNA'
medical.summary: A QIMR Berghofer-led team has developed a powerful tool to explore and understand the mysterious workings of the vast region of the human genome once dismissed as "junk DNA," discovering thousands of molecules that could hold the key to new precision cancer treatments.

medical.title: New mechanism shows how immune cells fine-tune adhesion during infection and recovery
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Liverpool helped uncover how the body adapts its immune defenses during periods of increased demand, such as infection, inflammation and recovery following stem cell transplantation.

medical.title: Babies face a higher death risk when their mother is experiencing intimate partner violence
medical.summary: Children whose mothers experience violence from a partner have a higher chance of dying before their fifth birthday, according to a major international study led by Curtin University. The research found that intimate partner violence was linked to a greater risk of babies and young children dying, highlighting how preventing violence against women could also help save children's lives.

medical.title: Fertility may drive a woman's desire for luxury
medical.summary: Hormonal fluctuations associated with fertility are associated with a greater tendency for women to use conspicuous luxury symbols, potentially to be noticed by men, according to a study published in PLOS One by Aekyoung Kim of Jeonbuk National University of the Republic of Korea and colleagues.

medical.title: Researchers investigate complex impact of mental health discussions on TikTok
medical.summary: In a new study, researchers have revealed the complex ways social media users engage with mental health and ADHD content on platforms like TikTok, with both positive and potentially negative impacts for users. Led by Dr. Katie Saunders from Keele University's School of Medicine, the paper, published in the Journal of Social Media Research, outlines the different ways TikTok users engage with mental health and ADHD content online, with a range of complex responses recorded.

medical.title: New class of KRAS inhibitors shows promise in shrinking NF1 nerve tumors
medical.summary: A scientist at Cincinnati Children's who has hunted for decades for ways to shrink the painful and disfiguring nerve tumors caused by neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) has made a new breakthrough in the quest. Nancy Ratner, Ph.D., and a team of nine co-authors are reporting that a novel class of medications—known as KRAS inhibitors—shows at least as much potential as FDA-approved MEK inhibitors in shrinking NF1 tumors.

medical.title: Scientists discover how fructose may help drive obesity
medical.summary: High-fructose corn syrup is just one of many food additives linked to obesity. It is typically found in sweetened beverages and processed foods and is added to enhance flavor and sweetness. However, exactly how it contributes to weight gain and obesity is not completely understood.

medical.title: Small spaces and stiffness may help cancer cells escape and spread
medical.summary: A new biomaterial developed by researchers from The University of Western Australia is providing fresh insights into the way cancer cells escape from tumors and spread through the body.

medical.title: ECG-based AI algorithm could improve detection and prediction of heart diseases
medical.summary: Clinicians often use a medical test called a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) to diagnose heart problems. It uses electrodes placed on the chest and limbs to record the heart's electrical activity. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are commonly used to assist with diagnoses based on ECGs. But current tools typically require large amounts of training data, hand-labeled with the presence or absence of specific diseases, which can make the tools less adaptable to other clinical tasks.

medical.title: Neuropsychologist finds gaps between treatment and science of ALS, dementia in her own family
medical.summary: For A. Campbell Sullivan, PsyD, this time it's personal. As a neuropsychologist and clinical associate professor of neurology at the Glenn Biggs Institute for Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases at UT Health San Antonio, she's on the front lines of groundbreaking research and patient care in frontotemporal dementia and other neurodegenerative disorders every day.

medical.title: Runner's high study finds cannabis-like signaling molecules rise over extreme distances
medical.summary: A marathon, 100 kilometers (62 miles) or even 230 kilometers (143 miles) in a single effort: Anyone running such distances puts enormous strain on their body. At the same time, levels of the body's own cannabis-like signaling molecules rise significantly. Dr. Michael Siebers from the Institute of Forensic Psychiatry and Sex Research at the University of Duisburg-Essen and his team have, for the first time, tracked in greater detail how these so-called endocannabinoids develop over the course of an entire marathon and during extreme ultramarathon distances. The study has been published in BMC Medicine.

medical.title: Top US doctors offer updated flu and COVID vaccine recommendations, aiming to ease confusion
medical.summary: Leading U.S. medical groups are urging people to get updated flu and COVID-19 vaccinations this fall, banding together Wednesday to issue shot guidelines—and highlight the science behind them—saying they hope to ease confusion caused by the Trump administration's changing advice.

medical.title: Understanding the link between neighborhood socioeconomic status and stroke recovery
medical.summary: In a 2021 study, Eric Stulberg, MD, MPH, assistant professor of neurology at Thomas Jefferson University, found an association between lower neighborhood socioeconomic status (nSES) and worse stroke recovery outcomes. "Even after accounting for individual economic status, as measured by their education level and insurance status, those in lower socioeconomic neighborhoods tend to have worse stroke recovery outcomes than those who are in the higher socioeconomic neighborhoods," Stulberg says.

medical.title: Co-designed counseling improves postpartum contraceptive choices, but organizational barriers remain
medical.summary: Becoming pregnant again soon after giving birth is associated with risks for both mother and child. A study led by Karolinska Institutet and published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology & Women's Health shows that approaches and guidance developed jointly by midwives and mothers can increase the proportion of women who choose effective contraception after childbirth, but also that organizational barriers limit opportunities for equitable care.

science.title: World must prepare for 'reality' of missing 1.5C goal: UN
science.summary: The United Nations said Wednesday the 1.5°C target would be missed and outlined how global temperatures might be brought back down in a first-of-its-kind assessment met with dismay in climate-vulnerable nations.

science.title: AI automates the creation of custom functional materials atom by atom
science.summary: Imagine a construction site where the bricks are individual molecules and the "cranes" are microscopic needles so sharp they can feel a single atom. For decades, building at this scale was a laborious, time-consuming task where a single human error could damage the delicate tools.

science.title: Belonging, atmosphere key to attracting event-goers
science.summary: Venues that become entwined in the cultural fabric of a community can be as enticing as the events they hold, according to University of the Sunshine Coast research.

science.title: Researchers identify the world's first cell line with the KMT2A::SEPTIN6 fusion gene
science.summary: Researchers at the Leibniz Institute DSMZ-German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures have, for the first time, identified a model cell line for a rare form of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). "The KOPM-88 cell line is, to date, the first and only known cell line worldwide to carry the KMT2A::SEPTIN6 fusion gene," explains Dr. Stefan Nagel, head of the Molecular Genetics research group in the Department of Human and Animal Cell Cultures at the DSMZ. "Thus, cancer research now has an urgently needed model system to specifically investigate this aggressive subtype of leukemia and develop novel therapeutic approaches." The work is published in the journal Cells.

science.title: A new layer of the human genome: Embedded RNA marks may reshape DNA twisting
science.summary: A new study led by Francesca Storici, a professor in the School of Biological Sciences and faculty member of the Parker H. Petit Institute for Bioengineering and Bioscience, has uncovered an unexpected feature of human DNA linked to gene activity and the physical organization of DNA. The findings, published in Cell, could change how scientists think about DNA organization, transcription and genome function.

science.title: Scientists observe Einstein's gravity in the quantum world
science.summary: An international team including Nobel Prize-winning physicist Professor Sir Roger Penrose has observed a long-predicted effect of gravity on a falling quantum object for the first time. The result shows that a fundamental principle at the heart of Einstein's theory of gravity remains consistent with the behavior of matter in the quantum world. The study, led by Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, the University of Ulm and the University of Oxford, was published today (Sept. 2) in Science Advances.

science.title: Weather shapes bus ridership, but cost and shelters can change the equation
science.summary: What makes someone decide to take—or skip—the bus on a cold, rainy, hot or smoky day?

science.title: Animal-bone records reveal how cattle and sheep fueled medieval England's changing economy
science.summary: As populations expanded in medieval England, key changes occurred in the uses of cattle and sheep to produce food and materials, according to a study published Sept. 2, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Matilda Holmes of the University of Leicester, United Kingdom, David Orton of the University of York, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

science.title: New nanostructure makes non-linear light conversion 72,000 times more efficient
science.summary: Researchers from Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), Harvard and the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin) have developed an innovative method for coupling light non-linearly. This opens up new possibilities for telecommunications and quantum technology.

science.title: Whether you're an introvert or extravert may decide how you should use AI
science.summary: More than a century ago, the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung made introversion and extraversion central to his theory of psychological types.

science.title: Sorry, this neutrino laser won't work, physicists say
science.summary: Neutrinos are pervasive yet intangible particles that permeate the universe, streaming through whole planets, stars and our bodies by the trillions each second. The elementary particles are often described as "ghostly" for their near-zero mass and elusive nature, as they have very little interaction with normal matter.

science.title: Dolphin-feeding tourism contributes to predicted dolphin decline
science.summary: A study published in the journal Oikos, titled "Forecasting the impact of food-provisioning and other stressors on a marine top-predator population," found that without protective management, the Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin population off Bunbury would fall from 350 to eight over 100 years.

science.title: When biology inspires mathematics: Hidden symmetries explain why widely used evolutionary methods can give false answers
science.summary: Why do some groups of organisms contain thousands of species while others have only a handful? Evolutionary biologists have spent decades trying to answer this question using mathematical models that estimate how biological traits and environmental factors influence the formation and extinction of species.

science.title: Wind-wave tunnel helps engineers dive deeper into ocean research
science.summary: Inside a lab at the University of Texas at Dallas, researchers have re-created a small-scale ocean environment where they can make waves build, break and crash into one another.

science.title: Iguanodon shinbone growth may be first evidence of an infected skin ulcer in a dinosaur
science.summary: Fossilized bones can reveal a wealth of details about animals, including their size, appearance, what they ate and any injuries they may have suffered. In a paper published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, researchers in Spain describe a swollen patch on the shinbone of an Iguanodon, which they say may be evidence of an advanced skin ulcer that had reached the underlying bone. If so, this could be the first time this type of response to a bacterial infection has been reported in a dinosaur.

science.title: How can we improve school attendance?
science.summary: Poor school attendance can negatively affect young people's behavior and future health. It is a growing public health concern because rates of persistent school absence have risen considerably and remained high in some parts of the country since the COVID-19 pandemic.

science.title: More trees are needed to cool down European cities in heat waves—but they must be planted near homes
science.summary: Heat waves claimed the lives of tens of thousands of people in Europe's capital cities this summer as they experienced record temperatures.

science.title: How cells teach themselves to move together
science.summary: Scientists have long wondered how cells organized into sheets begin to move together to form organs, especially when the sheets form closed, sphere-like surfaces and tissues with no edges to direct motion. Researchers at the University of Chicago and UC San Diego used a combination of live imaging, genetic experiments and mathematical modeling to understand how cells in the fruit fly egg chamber synchronize their movement.

science.title: New 'devil flower' species discovered in Thai national park
science.summary: Researchers have described a new species of leafless flowering plant found on the forest floor of a national park in western Thailand, and its otherworldly appearance has earned it a fittingly dramatic name: Thismia daemona, the "devil flower."

science.title: Rising Over Louisiana
science.summary: On Aug. 28, 2026 (the evening of Aug. 27 in some time zones), the Moon passed into Earth’s shadow, creating a deep partial lunar eclipse. At the moment of greatest eclipse, 12:13 a.m. EDT, 96.3% of the Moon’s disk was immersed in Earth’s umbra—the central, darkest part of the shadow where sunlight is completely blocked. […]

science.title: NASA Rocket Takes First Multi-Point Look Inside Radio-Disrupting Clouds
science.summary: High above Earth, thin veils of metallic haze drift through the edge of space. Known as sporadic E layers, these high-altitude “clouds” form from the vaporized dust of burnt-up meteors, earning their name from the unpredictable way they emerge and then dissipate. Now, new results from a NASA sounding rocket — a suborbital research rocket […]

With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

environment.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga

The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Lab-grown tissue reveals how inflammation may drive heart relaxation failure
mix_items.summary: Scientists study the underlying causes of a disease or test potential new drugs in animal models or cells obtained from human biopsy specimens before clinical trials. However, disease models in animals do not mimic actual human disease, and biopsy specimens are difficult to access for research purposes. Lab-grown tissues engineered from stem cells reprogrammed from human cells, called human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), are rapidly emerging as a more reliable and accessible model in medical research.

mix_items.title: Micro-LED mask improves skin elasticity beyond injections alone
mix_items.summary: Home beauty devices that allow users to care for their skin conveniently at home have grown popular recently, but conventional LED masks are limited by their rigid structures and point-emitting LEDs, which must be positioned away from the skin to spread light over a broader area. This inherently prevents close skin contact and increases optical loss.

mix_items.title: World must prepare for 'reality' of missing 1.5C goal: UN
mix_items.summary: The United Nations said Wednesday the 1.5°C target would be missed and outlined how global temperatures might be brought back down in a first-of-its-kind assessment met with dismay in climate-vulnerable nations.

mix_items.title: AI automates the creation of custom functional materials atom by atom
mix_items.summary: Imagine a construction site where the bricks are individual molecules and the "cranes" are microscopic needles so sharp they can feel a single atom. For decades, building at this scale was a laborious, time-consuming task where a single human error could damage the delicate tools.

mix_items.title: Belonging, atmosphere key to attracting event-goers
mix_items.summary: Venues that become entwined in the cultural fabric of a community can be as enticing as the events they hold, according to University of the Sunshine Coast research.

mix_items.title: Powerful new tool reveals potential 'goldmine' of cancer targets hidden in 'junk DNA'
mix_items.summary: A QIMR Berghofer-led team has developed a powerful tool to explore and understand the mysterious workings of the vast region of the human genome once dismissed as "junk DNA," discovering thousands of molecules that could hold the key to new precision cancer treatments.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify the world's first cell line with the KMT2A::SEPTIN6 fusion gene
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Leibniz Institute DSMZ-German Collection of Microorganisms and Cell Cultures have, for the first time, identified a model cell line for a rare form of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). "The KOPM-88 cell line is, to date, the first and only known cell line worldwide to carry the KMT2A::SEPTIN6 fusion gene," explains Dr. Stefan Nagel, head of the Molecular Genetics research group in the Department of Human and Animal Cell Cultures at the DSMZ. "Thus, cancer research now has an urgently needed model system to specifically investigate this aggressive subtype of leukemia and develop novel therapeutic approaches." The work is published in the journal Cells.

mix_items.title: New mechanism shows how immune cells fine-tune adhesion during infection and recovery
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Liverpool helped uncover how the body adapts its immune defenses during periods of increased demand, such as infection, inflammation and recovery following stem cell transplantation.

mix_items.title: Babies face a higher death risk when their mother is experiencing intimate partner violence
mix_items.summary: Children whose mothers experience violence from a partner have a higher chance of dying before their fifth birthday, according to a major international study led by Curtin University. The research found that intimate partner violence was linked to a greater risk of babies and young children dying, highlighting how preventing violence against women could also help save children's lives.

mix_items.title: A new layer of the human genome: Embedded RNA marks may reshape DNA twisting
mix_items.summary: A new study led by Francesca Storici, a professor in the School of Biological Sciences and faculty member of the Parker H. Petit Institute for Bioengineering and Bioscience, has uncovered an unexpected feature of human DNA linked to gene activity and the physical organization of DNA. The findings, published in Cell, could change how scientists think about DNA organization, transcription and genome function.

mix_items.title: Fertility may drive a woman's desire for luxury
mix_items.summary: Hormonal fluctuations associated with fertility are associated with a greater tendency for women to use conspicuous luxury symbols, potentially to be noticed by men, according to a study published in PLOS One by Aekyoung Kim of Jeonbuk National University of the Republic of Korea and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Scientists observe Einstein's gravity in the quantum world
mix_items.summary: An international team including Nobel Prize-winning physicist Professor Sir Roger Penrose has observed a long-predicted effect of gravity on a falling quantum object for the first time. The result shows that a fundamental principle at the heart of Einstein's theory of gravity remains consistent with the behavior of matter in the quantum world. The study, led by Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, the University of Ulm and the University of Oxford, was published today (Sept. 2) in Science Advances.

mix_items.title: Weather shapes bus ridership, but cost and shelters can change the equation
mix_items.summary: What makes someone decide to take—or skip—the bus on a cold, rainy, hot or smoky day?

mix_items.title: Researchers investigate complex impact of mental health discussions on TikTok
mix_items.summary: In a new study, researchers have revealed the complex ways social media users engage with mental health and ADHD content on platforms like TikTok, with both positive and potentially negative impacts for users. Led by Dr. Katie Saunders from Keele University's School of Medicine, the paper, published in the Journal of Social Media Research, outlines the different ways TikTok users engage with mental health and ADHD content online, with a range of complex responses recorded.

mix_items.title: New class of KRAS inhibitors shows promise in shrinking NF1 nerve tumors
mix_items.summary: A scientist at Cincinnati Children's who has hunted for decades for ways to shrink the painful and disfiguring nerve tumors caused by neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) has made a new breakthrough in the quest. Nancy Ratner, Ph.D., and a team of nine co-authors are reporting that a novel class of medications—known as KRAS inhibitors—shows at least as much potential as FDA-approved MEK inhibitors in shrinking NF1 tumors.

mix_items.title: Animal-bone records reveal how cattle and sheep fueled medieval England's changing economy
mix_items.summary: As populations expanded in medieval England, key changes occurred in the uses of cattle and sheep to produce food and materials, according to a study published Sept. 2, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Matilda Holmes of the University of Leicester, United Kingdom, David Orton of the University of York, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover how fructose may help drive obesity
mix_items.summary: High-fructose corn syrup is just one of many food additives linked to obesity. It is typically found in sweetened beverages and processed foods and is added to enhance flavor and sweetness. However, exactly how it contributes to weight gain and obesity is not completely understood.

mix_items.title: New nanostructure makes non-linear light conversion 72,000 times more efficient
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), Harvard and the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin) have developed an innovative method for coupling light non-linearly. This opens up new possibilities for telecommunications and quantum technology.

mix_items.title: Small spaces and stiffness may help cancer cells escape and spread
mix_items.summary: A new biomaterial developed by researchers from The University of Western Australia is providing fresh insights into the way cancer cells escape from tumors and spread through the body.

mix_items.title: Whether you're an introvert or extravert may decide how you should use AI
mix_items.summary: More than a century ago, the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung made introversion and extraversion central to his theory of psychological types.

mix_items.title: ECG-based AI algorithm could improve detection and prediction of heart diseases
mix_items.summary: Clinicians often use a medical test called a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) to diagnose heart problems. It uses electrodes placed on the chest and limbs to record the heart's electrical activity. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are commonly used to assist with diagnoses based on ECGs. But current tools typically require large amounts of training data, hand-labeled with the presence or absence of specific diseases, which can make the tools less adaptable to other clinical tasks.

mix_items.title: Sorry, this neutrino laser won't work, physicists say
mix_items.summary: Neutrinos are pervasive yet intangible particles that permeate the universe, streaming through whole planets, stars and our bodies by the trillions each second. The elementary particles are often described as "ghostly" for their near-zero mass and elusive nature, as they have very little interaction with normal matter.

mix_items.title: Neuropsychologist finds gaps between treatment and science of ALS, dementia in her own family
mix_items.summary: For A. Campbell Sullivan, PsyD, this time it's personal. As a neuropsychologist and clinical associate professor of neurology at the Glenn Biggs Institute for Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases at UT Health San Antonio, she's on the front lines of groundbreaking research and patient care in frontotemporal dementia and other neurodegenerative disorders every day.

mix_items.title: Dolphin-feeding tourism contributes to predicted dolphin decline
mix_items.summary: A study published in the journal Oikos, titled "Forecasting the impact of food-provisioning and other stressors on a marine top-predator population," found that without protective management, the Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin population off Bunbury would fall from 350 to eight over 100 years.

mix_items.title: When biology inspires mathematics: Hidden symmetries explain why widely used evolutionary methods can give false answers
mix_items.summary: Why do some groups of organisms contain thousands of species while others have only a handful? Evolutionary biologists have spent decades trying to answer this question using mathematical models that estimate how biological traits and environmental factors influence the formation and extinction of species.

mix_items.title: Runner's high study finds cannabis-like signaling molecules rise over extreme distances
mix_items.summary: A marathon, 100 kilometers (62 miles) or even 230 kilometers (143 miles) in a single effort: Anyone running such distances puts enormous strain on their body. At the same time, levels of the body's own cannabis-like signaling molecules rise significantly. Dr. Michael Siebers from the Institute of Forensic Psychiatry and Sex Research at the University of Duisburg-Essen and his team have, for the first time, tracked in greater detail how these so-called endocannabinoids develop over the course of an entire marathon and during extreme ultramarathon distances. The study has been published in BMC Medicine.

mix_items.title: Top US doctors offer updated flu and COVID vaccine recommendations, aiming to ease confusion
mix_items.summary: Leading U.S. medical groups are urging people to get updated flu and COVID-19 vaccinations this fall, banding together Wednesday to issue shot guidelines—and highlight the science behind them—saying they hope to ease confusion caused by the Trump administration's changing advice.

mix_items.title: Understanding the link between neighborhood socioeconomic status and stroke recovery
mix_items.summary: In a 2021 study, Eric Stulberg, MD, MPH, assistant professor of neurology at Thomas Jefferson University, found an association between lower neighborhood socioeconomic status (nSES) and worse stroke recovery outcomes. "Even after accounting for individual economic status, as measured by their education level and insurance status, those in lower socioeconomic neighborhoods tend to have worse stroke recovery outcomes than those who are in the higher socioeconomic neighborhoods," Stulberg says.

mix_items.title: Wind-wave tunnel helps engineers dive deeper into ocean research
mix_items.summary: Inside a lab at the University of Texas at Dallas, researchers have re-created a small-scale ocean environment where they can make waves build, break and crash into one another.

mix_items.title: Iguanodon shinbone growth may be first evidence of an infected skin ulcer in a dinosaur
mix_items.summary: Fossilized bones can reveal a wealth of details about animals, including their size, appearance, what they ate and any injuries they may have suffered. In a paper published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, researchers in Spain describe a swollen patch on the shinbone of an Iguanodon, which they say may be evidence of an advanced skin ulcer that had reached the underlying bone. If so, this could be the first time this type of response to a bacterial infection has been reported in a dinosaur.

mix_items.title: How can we improve school attendance?
mix_items.summary: Poor school attendance can negatively affect young people's behavior and future health. It is a growing public health concern because rates of persistent school absence have risen considerably and remained high in some parts of the country since the COVID-19 pandemic.

mix_items.title: More trees are needed to cool down European cities in heat waves—but they must be planted near homes
mix_items.summary: Heat waves claimed the lives of tens of thousands of people in Europe's capital cities this summer as they experienced record temperatures.

mix_items.title: How cells teach themselves to move together
mix_items.summary: Scientists have long wondered how cells organized into sheets begin to move together to form organs, especially when the sheets form closed, sphere-like surfaces and tissues with no edges to direct motion. Researchers at the University of Chicago and UC San Diego used a combination of live imaging, genetic experiments and mathematical modeling to understand how cells in the fruit fly egg chamber synchronize their movement.

mix_items.title: New 'devil flower' species discovered in Thai national park
mix_items.summary: Researchers have described a new species of leafless flowering plant found on the forest floor of a national park in western Thailand, and its otherworldly appearance has earned it a fittingly dramatic name: Thismia daemona, the "devil flower."

mix_items.title: Co-designed counseling improves postpartum contraceptive choices, but organizational barriers remain
mix_items.summary: Becoming pregnant again soon after giving birth is associated with risks for both mother and child. A study led by Karolinska Institutet and published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology & Women's Health shows that approaches and guidance developed jointly by midwives and mothers can increase the proportion of women who choose effective contraception after childbirth, but also that organizational barriers limit opportunities for equitable care.

mix_items.title: Rising Over Louisiana
mix_items.summary: On Aug. 28, 2026 (the evening of Aug. 27 in some time zones), the Moon passed into Earth’s shadow, creating a deep partial lunar eclipse. At the moment of greatest eclipse, 12:13 a.m. EDT, 96.3% of the Moon’s disk was immersed in Earth’s umbra—the central, darkest part of the shadow where sunlight is completely blocked. […]

mix_items.title: NASA Rocket Takes First Multi-Point Look Inside Radio-Disrupting Clouds
mix_items.summary: High above Earth, thin veils of metallic haze drift through the edge of space. Known as sporadic E layers, these high-altitude “clouds” form from the vaporized dust of burnt-up meteors, earning their name from the unpredictable way they emerge and then dissipate. Now, new results from a NASA sounding rocket — a suborbital research rocket […]

mix_items.summary: JANTHO, Indonesia — Illegal gold miners in Indonesia’s Aceh province have breached a crucial reintroduction forest for critically endangered Sumatran orangutans rescued from the illegal wildlife trade. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the […]

mix_items.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

satire_ro.title: Restaurant din Saturn, distins cu trei bacterii Michelin în prestigiosul ghid al toxiinfecţiei alimentare
